extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and television writers (WGA members and writers working under WGA jurisdiction) seeking to understand and protect their writing credit rights
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for determining writing credits on theatrical, television, and new media projects under the Writers Guild (MBA) jurisdiction, including eligibility, submission, arbitration, appeals, and related creative/publicity rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA coverage / signatory status
rubrics_metrics.description: Is your writing covered by the WGA? Make sure you are dealing with a signatory company (Company) meaning that the company is signatory to, and bound by, the WGA Theatrical and Television Basic Agreement (MBA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guild Working Rules prohibit members from working for or selling to a non-signatory. Call the Guild's Signatories Department to check status—do not rely on an agent or the company's representations. If your agreement is with a non-signatory, you may not be eligible to compete for writing credit even if the project later becomes covered by the MBA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional writer status for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are optioning or selling material to a signatory company, you must be considered a 'professional writer' to be eligible for writing credit (unless employed by the signatory to render writing services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MBA generally defines a 'professional writer' as someone who has received employment for a total of thirteen weeks as a television or theatrical motion picture writer, or received credit as a writer on a television or theatrical motion picture (including series), or credit for a professionally produced play or a published novel. You may negotiate to be treated as a professional writer even if you don't meet these criteria; Guild membership alone does not automatically qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of other writers and source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there other writers on the project? Article 18 requires a Company to notify you of any writer assigned to the same project whether prior, concurrent, or (in some circumstances) subsequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether invitations have been extended to other writers and whether there is assigned source material. This affects likelihood of credit and whether you are a first or subsequent writer. Use the Article 18 Notice form to request information; do not rely on the Company to volunteer it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production executive status affects credit
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are employed as a director, producer, or (in episodic television) a story editor, or negotiate producer credit, then when credits are determined you will be subject to specific rules pertaining to production executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing credits involving production executives are subject to automatic arbitration provisions; in screen arbitrations for 'original screenplays' the percentage necessary for a production executive to receive credit may be higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover page format and required attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover pages of each piece of material must include the name of the first writer followed by the word 'revisions' and then names of all subsequent writers. Subsequent writers should indicate contributions with 'current revisions by' plus name and date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover page tracks who the writers are and who is responsible for changes in that specific document. Do not remove names of earlier writers even if you think none of their words remain. Failure to adhere to cover page requirements violates Guild working rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document delivery and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep copies of all material submitted and accurate records of delivery; Arbitration Committee can consider only literary material submitted to the Company or an authorized representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach cover memos/emails noting recipient, date, and description. Guild registration is not proof of delivery to the Company. Deliver a filmography with your final draft to help ensure inclusion in publicity if credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and rules for writing teams
rubrics_metrics.description: A team is two or more writers assigned at about the same time to the same material who work together for approximately the same length of time. Team member names are separated by an ampersand (&).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams cannot split joint work into separate solo pieces. No more than three writers may form a team unless waived; a team is a separate and distinct writer for arbitration purposes. If one team member is a production executive, a written collaboration agreement approved by the Guild is required. If you object to a claimed team, take affirmative steps (cover page, notify Company, contact Credits Department) rather than waiting for arbitration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Tentative Writing Credits (NTWC) and FSS requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of principal photography the Company must send a Notice of Tentative Writing Credits (NTWC) and a copy of the final shooting script (FSS) to the Guild and each participating writer. The NTWC lists participating writers, proposed credits, and any source credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't receive an NTWC after principal photography, contact the Guild immediately. Residuals and ancillary rights are based on credit; missing NTWC can delay payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain current contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the Company and the Guild have your current address so NTWC and FSS are delivered timely; agent forwarding does not relieve you of responsibility to receive notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your contract directs notices to an agent, ensure the agent forwards notices promptly and update the Company in writing when your representation changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit name accuracy and pseudonym registration
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing the NTWC make sure your name appears exactly as it is on file with the Guild; writers must take credit exactly as in Guild records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may use a 'reasonable' pseudonym if registered with the Guild; Guild can object later if the pseudonym is unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimous agreement among writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where more than one writer or team participates, all participating writers have the right to agree unanimously among themselves as to which of them shall receive writing credit (unless automatic arbitration is required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreed forms of credit must be in accordance with the MBA and reached in advance of arbitration. Notify Credits staff if you would agree to particular credit so they can facilitate communication among writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protests, deadlines, and automatic arbitration triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's timely protest of the Company's proposed tentative credits typically triggers a Guild arbitration. The NTWC will list the protest deadline; failure to protest by that date lets tentative credits become final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send a written protest to the Guild and Company stating you are protesting, naming the production, and how you believe credits should read. Automatic arbitration occurs in specified instances (e.g., production executive proposed for writing credit with non-production executive participating writers; three writers proposed to share certain 'by' credits; 'Screen Story by' or 'Television Story by' credit proposed; 'Adaptation by' proposed; in television, 'Developed by' proposed on a series with separated rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participating writer investigation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When investigating whether someone is entitled to be listed as a participating writer, the Guild looks to whether the writer wrote under Guild jurisdiction, whether the literary material is owned by the producing company, and whether the project on which the writer performed services and the Picture are the same project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A participating writer investigation decides only entitlement to review FSS and to compete for credit, not whether the writer deserves credit. If the Guild finds entitlement, it instructs Company to submit a revised NTWC or may submit the matter to legal arbitration if Company disagrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remake investigation and remake definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A remake investigation decides whether a film is a remake of an earlier film produced under Guild jurisdiction. A remake is generally defined as a motion picture containing substantial similarity to a prior motion picture with respect to principal characters, general setting, plot, storyline, tone, events, and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original was under Guild jurisdiction, credited writers of the original are considered participating writers on the remake and are eligible to compete for writing credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Reader role and use
rubrics_metrics.description: An Expert Reader is used to analyze literary material and give an opinion on issues (e.g., whether a picture is a remake, whether material changes warrant reopening credits, whether projects are sufficiently similar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert Readers are experienced writers drawn from a pool, generally served as arbiters, and may act as Guild expert witnesses in legal arbitration. An Expert Reader will not serve in other capacities in the same credits determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Arbitration hearing subject-matter (materials disputes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Request a Pre-Arbitration hearing to resolve disputes about the materials to be considered in a credit arbitration (chronological sequence, authenticity, authorship, completeness, identification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All issues related to materials must be resolved before sending materials to the Arbitration Committee. Participating writers should review the list of materials and verify items like proper dating, sequencing, authorship attribution, and whether submitted materials are literary or source material (research is not 'source material'). Failure to challenge materials before submission is not ground for overturning an Arbitration Committee decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Arbitration hearing process
rubrics_metrics.description: A Special Committee of three Guild members (also TV/Screen Credits Committee members) conducts the Pre-Arbitration Hearing; the requesting writer meets first, then other writers meet individually; Guild staff provides relevant agreements and policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearings are generally informal; bringing a representative is optional. These panelists also serve as members of the TV or Screen Credits Committee and their decisions are time-sensitive due to MBA arbitration timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Special Committee decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Special Committee's decisions (e.g., on sequencing) must be followed by the Arbitration Committee and participating writers; writers cannot reference contrary information in arbitration statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you disagree with a Special Committee decision you may raise it on appeal to a Policy Review Board after arbitration; disagreement may become moot if credit outcome makes it so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits Manual rules and percentage thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the Credits Manuals carefully: Screen Credits Manual and Television Credits Manual set specific quantitative and qualitative rules for awarding credits (including percent contribution thresholds for 'Screenplay' credit depending on original/non-original status and first/subsequent or production executive status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example table for theatrical motion pictures: First Writer – Non Production Executive: >33% (original & non-original); Subsequent Writer – Non Production Executive: 50% (original), >33% (non-original); thresholds differ if production executive. Television teleplay credit uses 'substantially more' for subsequent writers on one of four teleplay elements. Refer to Appendices A and B for breakdowns and to request the Manuals if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines and timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of, and adhere to, all deadlines—the Guild's exclusive authority to determine credits exists for a specified number of days and there is a deadline for every step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are strict timelines throughout (NTWC protest deadline, time to prepare statements, 24-hour appeal windows, MBA timeframes). Missing deadlines can forfeit rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material verification and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Company must submit three copies of each writer's literary materials and all source material; 'Literary Material' includes stories, treatments, screenplays, teleplays, sketches, outlines, etc.; 'Source Material' includes underlying works like novels, comic books, stage plays. Research is not source material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credits staff will contact writers to verify completeness; participating writers must verify accuracy before materials are sent to Arbitration Committee and provide missing materials within time frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding and anonymity in arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: All credit arbitrations are 'coded'—names of writers are not revealed to the Arbitration Committee; writers are referred to by letter codes (Writer A, Writer B, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In team cases, the team is coded as a single writer; individual team members who also write independently receive different letter designations. Statements must avoid revealing identities or whether a writer was a production executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration statement guidance, limits, and prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers may submit a statement to the Arbitration Committee (Screen: recommended 1–5 single-spaced pages; Television: not exceed three single-spaced pages). Statements should focus on contributions as they remain in the FSS and avoid extraneous development process information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibited content includes references to entitlement to contingent compensation, letters/comments of support, irrelevant information that may prejudice, identity-revealing information, anything contradicting Special Committee decisions, prior proceedings, or any material not admissible. Statements must be submitted within specified windows (Screen: 72 hours from notification that materials are submitted; Television: 24 hours after notice), may request reasonable extensions, and should be personally written (Guild discourages 'statement experts'). See Appendix C for more guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to delete arbiters from list
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating writer is provided a list of eligible arbiters and may delete a reasonable number of names for any reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guild does not inquire why names are deleted; deletions are to allow strikes for perceived bias or prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration Committee composition and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Arbitration Committee consists of three Guild members with eligibility outlined in Credits Manuals; each committee is assigned a consultant and arbiter identities are confidential (they are unknown to each other and to writers/company).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultants are experienced members who can advise on rules and policy; confidentiality is maintained to prevent retaliation or outside pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of materials to Arbitration Committee and cover memo contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating writer may submit any or all of their verified literary materials (only their own); typically submit only drafts necessary for arbiters to assess contributions (often just the FSS for the last writer). The Arbitration Committee also receives writers' statements, the Credits Manual, and a cover memo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cover memo includes the tentative writing credits from the NTWC, a chronological list of writers' materials, references to applicable rules specifying required contributions for credits, and the deadline for the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration Committee decision process and appeal window
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbiters read materials, deliberate independently, then report decisions; if not unanimous, they teleconference and try to reach consensus; majority decision becomes the committee's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After notification, each writer has 24 hours to appeal by requesting a Policy Review Board. If no PRB request within the 24-hour windows of all writers, Arbitration Committee's decision becomes final. Writers can request copies of arbiters' written opinions (identities withheld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Review Board (PRB) scope and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 24 hours of receiving notice of the Arbitration Committee's decision, a participating writer may request a PRB. The PRB is a procedural review and may consider only whether there was any serious deviation from Guild policy or procedure in how the arbitration was conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRB cannot reverse arbiter judgment calls about literary analysis. Concurrent with a PRB request, writers should submit a written statement setting forth the grounds for the request as outlined in the Credits Manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRB process
rubrics_metrics.description: PRB panel consists of three Guild members from the Television or Screen Credits Committee; prior to hearing the PRB reviews arbiters' written decisions and writers' statements but does NOT read or analyze the literary materials submitted to the Arbitration Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearings are informal; writer meets with panel first and other writers respond. If a Pre-Arbitration ruling was challenged, the PRB reviews that decision and all material submitted to the Special Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRB decision outcomes and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If PRB finds no violation of policy/procedure the Arbitration Committee decision becomes final. If it finds a violation, PRB may (1) send materials back to the original Arbitration Committee for reconsideration (with clarification), or (2) direct Guild staff to form a new Arbitration Committee to re-determine credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a second Arbitration Committee is formed, participating writers may again appeal that second decision to a PRB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final credits binding and publicity compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the Guild makes a final determination of credits, the Company and all participating writers must abide by the Guild's decision; advertising, publicity, and on-screen credits must comport with the Guild-determined final credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may not claim credit contrary to the Guild's final credits. Report inaccurate or incorrect writing credits immediately to the Guild. The Company may use NTWC credits in publicity prior to final determination in good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing credits on episodic series with separated rights ('Created by' and 'Developed by')
rubrics_metrics.description: On series with separated rights, 'Created by' credit and separated rights are accorded to writers with 'Written by' or 'Story by' credit on the pilot and/or the writer(s) of the series format. 'Developed by' credit is not automatic and has specific requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Developed by' requires (1) Company agreement to propose you, (2) automatic arbitration to determine appropriateness, and (3) that the writer be eligible for but not entitled to 'Created by', or have 'Teleplay by' credit on the pilot, or have 'contributed to the distinctiveness and viability of the series.' For reboots, if reboot uses same format, original separated rights and 'Created by' may carry over; Expert Readers may be used to assess format sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing credits on series with no separated rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no separated rights in a series, continuing credits are purely contractual—given only if the writer contracted to receive such credit and no MBA benefits attach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guild prefers qualifiers for continuing credits (e.g., 'Developed for Television' or 'Series Created by' for high-budget SVOD) when appropriate; series based on previously exploited material typically have no separated rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative rights — viewing cuts and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating writers on theatrical motion pictures must be given the opportunity to view a cut of the film in sufficient time for any approved editing suggestions to be reasonably and effectively implemented. For long-form television/multi-part closed-end series, invite to view 'Director's cut' within 48 hours or supply videocassette simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing must allow for effective implementation of editing suggestions. Negotiation in individual contracts may secure better terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative rights — premieres, sneak previews, and travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Credited writers on theatrical motion pictures must be invited to the domestic premiere or first domestic festival and to the first sneak preview (if any) in LA County for pilots, long-form, or multi-part series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If travel exceeds 150 miles, Company must provide first class travel and accommodations. Where possible, give five days' notice of sneak previews. Individual contracts may negotiate better terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative rights — press junkets and publicity inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Credited writers must be invited to domestic press junkets for theatrical motion pictures; if required to travel more than 150 miles to junkets, Company must provide first class travel and accommodations. Identity, background, and filmography must be included in press kits/DVD/web pages if similar director information is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the director is interviewed for the press kit/DVD, the writer must also be interviewed unless otherwise notified. Writers should submit biography/filmography to advertising/publicity at time of last material submission.
